title: Building the next generation of AI developer tools

segments.text: Uh hello everyone. Everyone excited? Everyone happy after lunch? Full of energy? Yeah. Okay. Lovely. So, my talk is going to be about the next generation of
developer tools. And obviously nowadays next generation of developer tools, it needs to be about AI. Uh I'm software developer by trade. I've been working on developer tools for last
15 years of my life. Uh initially as a just open source person doing a lot of independent open source projects in this area. And then
for the last 5 years I've been part of GitHub Next. What I helped to create tools like original GitHub Copilot or Copilot next that it suggestion or couple of newer
tools like agentic workflows or A's which I'll I will mention later today. Uh so, probably your question right now is what is GitHub Next? I've heard about
GitHub, but what the hell is GitHub Next? And Next is this group inside GitHub that is responsible for investigating the future. The future of software
development, the future of GitHub as a platform. We are very small group of researchers and developers. There is 15 of us right now in the in
the group and we try to push boundaries and go where no one has gone before. Well, at least in context of developer tools. Uh our tools varies. We created a family
of fonts called Mona Space that got very popular. It's very innovative family of fonts for software developers. I'm actually using the fonts here in this
presentation. So, on the one hand we have projects like fonts. On the other hand we have projects like original Copilot and all the AI stuff. There is one core thing in
there. We The only thing we care about is developer happiness, developer experience, and developer productivity. We are not here to I'm not here to sell
you anything. I'm not here to tell you about latest greatest product that you pay GitHub money for. You can go there and talk with people at booth to do
that. I'm researcher. As such, I do not represent GitHub or Microsoft as a whole. Uh at best, I represent myself at in worst case, I represent GitHub next. So, I
have absolutely no idea about our product strategy, about our pricing. I don't know why Copilot is suddenly so expensive or why we have less than two nines of availability. All
those questions there. Uh So, I've promised in abstract and then in in this introduction that I will talk about future of software development. But talking about future
is difficult. So, let's take it step by step. And let's talk about software development first in general. As a developers, I imagine that vast
majority of us in this room are developers and we love to talk about technology, about programming languages, about weird tools. And we have all this magical
lingo that we use that exists only for sake of confusing those normal people that are outside of our group in here. But when you take all this away,
you are just left with basically two main components. Collaborative problem solving and then also collaborative manufacturing or building. Uh you get bunch of people
together in single room, in a single Slack channel, depends on how you work. Those are developers, product managers, project owners, whatever fancy titles people have, UI designers, lawyers,
business experts. And you tell them to figure something out, to solve some problem for your users. Uh and then after they figure it out, you
tell us probably slightly different group of people to get together and execute and build software. As such, this is not really different from any other business process. Like
again, like we as a developers, we love to talk about technology, but those core principles are not so much different than what we've observed
in the history of whole industry and whole manufacturing. And there's also one very big axiom about software development. It is that software development has always been
changing. We love to focus on current moment in time. We love to tell people that, you know, there is this AI hype wave and it
changes everything. But you know, if you go back in time to 5 years ago when we were starting original GitHub Copilot, when you look
at the state of the software development back then, it was totally different than state of the software development 20 years ago when I was starting my career or my
adventure with programming. Uh and then it was even crazier 40 years ago or 60 years ago. We've changed everything, tools, methodologies, programming languages. We
went from punch cards to assembler to higher programming languages and nowadays probably markdown is the main programming languages of the future. We went from having servers in the same
room as our office just next door to having cloud. We went from Microsoft executives telling us that Linux is cancer to now having Linux being part of
Windows. Uh and Microsoft loving open source. So, the only constant is change. Because of that constant change, making predictions about the future is very difficult. Uh there are infinite
amounts of possible futures. Uh I can make any random bet right now today that tomorrow we will invent uh faster than light travel or something
like that, but that doesn't make this bet this this opinion I've just phrased really interesting. What is interesting for me as a researcher is looking for
those futures that are possible to happen and those that are preferable for my goals. This is like technique called speculative decoding speculative design speculative decoding
is something else. >> [laughter] >> Speculative design that is very much used in like product design and we use that a lot also in in our work.
So to pick up those futures that are possible and preferable for our goals, we need to have set of assumptions and guidelines that will guide us
that will let us choose the right options to investigate out of any set of possible bets. And there is no better place to look at
those guidelines than our past. We look at what succeeded and what didn't work. We look at mistakes we've made. We've developed over last 5 years we've developed
maybe 10 open source maybe 10 AI products and only some of them were actually successful on the market. We developed even more prototypes probably countless number of prototypes
because like basically what we do in our work basically every every week we have this like demo meeting and we show new prototypes to
our team of cool stuff that we build on the side while working on on on main product that we are building. So we are building all this stuff and we
can look at what worked. We can generalize the lessons. We can we can make some assumptions. Anyone remembers this user experience? It's original GitHub Copilot the the
tool that started this whole AI adventure and it has been designed in very extreme way. And I say that in good way because I'm
kind of like I'm proud of this design. I I've helped to build it. And the goal here was one single thing keeping developers in the state of the
flow while they code by reducing the amount of context switching that they had to do. Our competitor, when we were building that, our competition was not other IDE,
it was not other tool inside your editor, it was Stack Overflow. Because 5 years ago, what you did when you were stuck on something, you were Googling
and the first result was was result from Stack Overflow and you took code from there and you copy-pasted it in your into your editor. But this whole process
of moving away from your editor, of Googling, of looking at the example at result and from Stack Overflow, trying to understand if it's the right answer
and seeing that oh, this question is closed because it's unproductive. Uh this killed your flow as a developer. And also this user experience has been
result of the constraints that we had. Models back then were absolutely terrible. Uh even in this very constrained use case, which was like showing just couple of lines of code at
most at the location of your cursor, we had something like 30% accuracy rate originally. Absolutely terrible number. Right now, we have, you know, those
super smart models having like 90% success rates at very difficult task in very difficult benchmarks. Uh But despite the fact that everything is different on the model side, some of the
core assumptions are still here, still still the same. And the first biggest one is that AI is not perfect and it will never be
perfect. AI by design is is probabilistic model. This is like what AI is. Because of that, it will always have some capability of hallucinate. We try to minimize that
capability, but it's always there. Uh it doesn't know what is truth or it's what is not true. Like, it will tell you one thing and then you will point at
some mistake and it will be like, "Oh, yes, you're absolutely right." It cannot count how many Rs are in strawberry, right? So, we need to we need to design those
systems in a way that that fights this. But, that doesn't mean that AI is useless. Because like in the social media, you see a lot of
discussion where people divided themselves into two groups, AI enthusiasts and AI doomers, and they fight like it's rooting for like sports teams or something like that. This is
not the case. You can still be very enthusiastic about AI tools like me, while acknowledging that we need to design systems using AI in very specific
way. And the main thing is, well, maybe not the main, but one of the very important things is designing systems defensively for failure. This is something that we know as
software developers, uh but we apply that on very tactical, low-level kind of like we need to handle exception in our code and so on. Uh we need to make sure
that our whole system doesn't die when database goes offline. Uh but, here the failure is slightly different. Because, even if one, well, one of the failure modes is that model
hallucinated answer. But, then even if the answer is technically correct, it still may be wrong answer. Because slight miscommunications impact even human-to-human relationships and
human-to-human processes and human-to-human decision-making. So, this is even worse with like magical black box that will do whatever you tell it to do, however it understands what
you just told it. Uh so, all the suggestions, I have couple of rules here that I like to apply to my my projects, and those are just
suggestions. But, basically, all the output of the AI should be reviewable by users. Suggestions or answers from AI should never be like automatically applied to
living systems. They should never be like, "Oh, it will make transfer of money for like $5,000 for me." It shouldn't be capable of just deleting my GitHub
repository or so on. Like, those steps, maybe those are the right steps, but you need to have user in the loop, human in the loop that will confirm that this is
exactly what you wanted. Suggestions should be or answers should be easy to ignore if they're wrong. They should be easy to retry or iterate
on because again slight miscommunications happen, but sometimes the best way out of the of slight miscommunication is just continuing conversation. Uh and also the suggestions preferably
should be easy to modify. And all those points can be implemented in various different user experiences. With original Copilot, you could just kept typing if suggestion was wrong. There
was zero cost for wrong suggestion. In case of chats and agents, like, you know, you can iterate with next message. Uh some of the harnesses gives you
ability to revert message, to fork conversation, and so on. And another very important thing to to to to keep in mind is that human creativity is unparalleled. Humans
are know other humans best. Uh Lena had absolutely awesome talk at the main stage uh earlier today about touching this problem of the problem of if we can
build anything, how should we know what we should build? Uh and only humans will know what to build. Only humans will understand what the
problems other people have. Only humans will understand uh what is worth solving. As such, our tools always need to enhance user capabilities rather than be
about replacing humans. There is a lot of talk about AI replacing developers. This is not the future we try to create. And also very important thing that we've
noticed, especially with the rise of agents, is that vast majority of tasks are in software development that are highly ambiguous. That's why we are paid a lot of money as
developers. That's why our staff developers or principal developers are so good at their job. It's that because they can figure out values ambiguity that tasks. It's very easy to create
demo of agent doing some hello world, you know, change color of frame to something else or center the div because that's funny because no one can knows
how to center div. So, but those are not real tasks. In practice, vast majority of tasks requires exploration, iteration, facing, clarifications, uh getting input from multiple actors, not
only from single developer. And because of that, systems using AI still need constant guidance and adjustment and and this is like human guidance and human and human
doing the adjustments. Another thing that I think we we can all agree looking at this whole this conference and looking at other talks is that the code is very cheap today.
Agents are capable of generating awesome codes, really good technical code, and they generate it way faster. They probably, you know, maybe there are some
niche scenarios where I can still outcode agent, but in vast majority of simple cases of normal code, agents will be better than me and will be faster
than me. Uh as an as anecdote, I can tell you that last time I've written line of code manually by hand in my editor was in
December last year. So, it's like what, 7 months of 100% of my code is written by agents. While software development has never been about just mechanical act of
coding, like we are getting paid a lot of money for our problem-solving capability, mechanical act of coding was always there and it was something that
we had to spend time on. And now we don't. Uh So, as long as we know what we want to build, we can build anything. That
sounds great, right? But we need to figure it out how to do that. So, now let's finally, after half of the talk, let's slowly move towards future.
When I look at trajectory of AI tools, it's very clear that the more powerful tools and more powerful models we have, we up the layer of abstraction. So, we
moved from very localized changes with AI in case of original Copilot when it was just code suggestion at your cursor position to now agent have capability of
like easily working on your even big repositories. However, our organizations doesn't just have single repository. Some startups do have and that's why they see those amazing productivity
gains from AI because they have small products and so they can very quickly iterate with AI. This is true. But for vast majority of like existing
companies, brownfield companies, it's thousands upon thousands of repositories with not only hundreds of like code projects, but also with like context and knowledge of the company put into
various location. So, we need to figure out how to move this higher level of abstraction. At the same time, when I look at the
most AI developer tools today, they are focused on on individual productivity. We make single developer be capable of running really fast. But running really fast is probably not
the best way to scale the process as a whole. So, let's go back to this my original definition, and specifically let's focus on on process of building software, of
manufacturing, of executing. Uh but looking at our history of humankind, like we we can easily observe that we don't you don't scale manufacturing by
running faster as a individuals. What you do, you build factories. What are factories? Factories are automated processes that you can introduce to the to the to the pipeline.
And our take for that is this concept that we've coined called continuous AI. Uh probably as the name suggests, it's similar to continuous integration,
continuous delivery. So, it is about running AI workflows uh automatically based on some triggers, just like normal CI/CD. What is different is that with CI or CD, you are
limited to what you can script, to to very small things. With AI, you can do anything. Do you want to have daily report about
uh activity in your repository? Sure, you can do that. Do you want to have agent every day checking uh if test coverage has moved into the the right
direction and or send you pull request improving the test coverage. You can easily do that. Do Anything like that is possible with AI. But when we run
agents automatically based on some triggers, that obviously means less human supervision. The human supervision will be there at the last step of the process, but it's less
than you checking every step in your editor. That means that things like security and AI ops have become very important. On this track, earlier today we had uh
one talk about that, uh which was like very close to to to our take on on on on security and AI ops for automated AI agents.
Organizations, especially the bigger the organization the the truer this take is, they cannot just release agents in the wild because, you know, code is valuable, their repositories are
valuable, their data databases are valuable. So, you know, last thing you want is getting your agent prompt injected and uploading all the secrets from your repository to some
external server. Or even if you just run open source project and you run use AI agent to help you help you maintain it, the last thing
you want is to spam every issue of the on the project because that will just annoy the users. That will not be helpful. So, because of that, what you want is
you want to have ability to limit what your AI agents can do, uh make sure that those limits are actually true and they hold. And those limits
needs to apply in deterministic way. So, they cannot be part of your prompt toward to AI agent, but they need to be deterministic checks around your AI
agent. And we have project for that that we are working on at next and it's called GitHub agentic workflows. Uh I will not go into details. Uh
